claims.evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy and western blotting data showing absence of mitochondrial localization for AURKA ΔNter, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claims.claim: AURKA ΔNter did not interact with TOMM.
claims.source: However, an AURKA truncation mutant in which the first 30 amino acids were removed (AURKA ΔNter) did not localise to mitochondria by confocal microscopy and western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B) and did not interact with TOMM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), although catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA (Lim et al., 2010; Kashatus et al., 2011; Bertolin et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing no interaction between AURKA ΔNter and TOMM, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: AURKA ΔNter is catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA.
claims.source: However, an AURKA truncation mutant in which the first 30 amino acids were removed (AURKA ΔNter) did not localise to mitochondria by confocal microscopy and western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B) and did not interact with TOMM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), although catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA (Lim et al., 2010; Kashatus et al., 2011; Bertolin et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on in vitro kinase assay data showing AURKA ΔNter phosphorylates histone H3 and RALA, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The depletion of RALA does not inhibit the entry of AURKA into mitochondria.
claims.source: We observed that the depletion of RALA does not inhibit the entry of AURKA into mitochondria. However, it impacts the abundance of AURKA to the same extent in total fractions and inside mitochondria. Therefore, the mitochondrial import of AURKA is RALA-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing AURKA in mitochondria after RALA depletion, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial import of AURKA is RALA-independent.
claims.source: We observed that the depletion of RALA does not inhibit the entry of AURKA into mitochondria. However, it impacts the abundance of AURKA to the same extent in total fractions and inside mitochondria. Therefore, the mitochondrial import of AURKA is RALA-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RALA depletion does not prevent AURKA mitochondrial localization.

claims.claim: AURKA38 was detected in cytosolic fractions of HEK293 cells, indicating that the kinase is exported from mitochondria after processing.
claims.source: Intriguingly, AURKA38 was also detected in cytosolic fractions of HEK293 cells, indicating that the kinase is exported from mitochondria after processing (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing AURKA38 in cytosolic fractions, shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: MitoAURKA (AURKA with the first 30 amino acids replaced with a strong MTS from cytochrome c oxidase) was not exported back to the cytosol.
claims.source: To establish whether this feature is intrinsic to the AURKA MTS, we replaced the first 30 amino acids of AURKA with a well characterised, strong MTS derived from cytochrome c oxidase, which is known to be recognised by TOMM and cleaved by PMPCB (Chacinska et al., 2009). This yields an exclusively mitochondrial AURKA (mitoAURKA), which was not exported back to the cytosol (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing mitoAURKA exclusively in mitochondrial fractions, shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3C.

claims.claim: MitoAURKA did not localise at the centrosome when compared to normal AURKA.
claims.source: In addition, mitoAURKA did not localise at the centrosome when compared to normal AURKA (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy data comparing centrosomal localization of AURKA and mitoAURKA, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The AURKA biosensor localises at mitochondria as endogenous AURKA in MCF7 cells does.
claims.source: The AURKA biosensor localises at mitochondria as endogenous AURKA in MCF7 cells does (Figure 2D,E and see Figure 1A for comparison), and the decrease in the lifetime of GFP revealed that it is autophosphorylated on Thr288 and activated in mitochondria.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on FLIM microscopy data showing the biosensor at mitochondria, shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: The AURKA biosensor is autophosphorylated on Thr288 and activated in mitochondria.
claims.source: The AURKA biosensor localises at mitochondria as endogenous AURKA in MCF7 cells does (Figure 2D,E and see Figure 1A for comparison), and the decrease in the lifetime of GFP revealed that it is autophosphorylated on Thr288 and activated in mitochondria.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing decreased GFP lifetime, indicating autophosphorylation and activation, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The activation of the AURKA biosensor in mitochondria is abolished by the AURKA inhibitor Alisertib (MLN8237).
claims.source: This activation is abolished by the AURKA inhibitor Alisertib (MLN8237) (Figure 2D), an ATP-analogue currently under clinical trials (Görgün et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing no decrease in GFP lifetime upon MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 2D, and supported by citation.

claims.claim: A kinase-dead mutant of AURKA (AURKA Lys162Met) was not retrieved in mitochondrial fractions.
claims.source: In this light, we assessed whether a kinase-dead mutant of AURKA (AURKA Lys162Met) could shuttle to mitochondria. Indeed, AURKA Lys162Met was not retrieved in mitochondrial fractions (Figure 2F), indicating that the kinase activity of AURKA is required for its mitochondrial localisation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing absence of AURKA Lys162Met in mitochondrial fractions, shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The kinase activity of AURKA is required for its mitochondrial localisation.
claims.source: In this light, we assessed whether a kinase-dead mutant of AURKA (AURKA Lys162Met) could shuttle to mitochondria. Indeed, AURKA Lys162Met was not retrieved in mitochondrial fractions (Figure 2F), indicating that the kinase activity of AURKA is required for its mitochondrial localisation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that kinase-dead AURKA does not localize to mitochondria.

claims.claim: Knockdown of AURKA led to mitochondrial elongation with swollen organelles showing intact cristae and no apparent loss of intramitochondrial content.
claims.source: First, we analysed mitochondrial morphology by TEM in HEK293 cells. Knockdown of AURKA led to mitochondrial elongation: the organelles appeared swollen, but they showed intact cristae and no apparent loss of intramitochondrial content (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on transmission electron microscopy data showing mitochondrial morphology changes upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The silencing of AURKA increases the length of the whole mitochondrial network.
claims.source: Analyses of mitochondrial length and branching (Koopman et al., 2005) revealed that the silencing of AURKA increases the length of the whole mitochondrial network (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), confirming previous results obtained with a kinase-dead version of AURKA (Kashatus et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial morphology, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, and supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: When AURKA is over-expressed, mitochondria are interconnected and they pack into mitochondrial clusters.
claims.source: Intriguingly, TEM analyses showed that mitochondria interconnectivity increases also when AURKA is over-expressed, again with no apparent signs of intramitochondrial content loss (Figure 3A). Under these conditions, analyses of mitochondrial network morphology showed that mitochondria are interconnected and they pack into mitochondrial clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on TEM and morphological analysis data showing mitochondrial clustering upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: AURKA loss-of-function mutants or those harbouring an AURKA-targeted RNAi and gain-of-function mutants (overexpression of Drosophila AURKA) showed more interconnected mitochondria than did controls in Drosophila.
claims.source: AURKA loss-of-function mutants or those harbouring an AURKA-targeted RNAi and gain-of-function mutants (overexpression of Drosophila AURKA) showed more interconnected mitochondria than did controls (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C, red panels).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data in Drosophila showing increased mitochondrial connectivity, shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: Mitochondria are interconnected in MCF7 cells both when AURKA is silenced or over-expressed.
claims.source: By using the diffusion of red mitoDendra2, we confirmed that mitochondria are interconnected also in MCF7 cells both when AURKA is silenced or over-expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data in MCF7 cells, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial interconnectivity in the presence of over-expressed AURKA depends on its capacity to be imported/exported, and on the kinase activity of AURKA itself.
claims.source: We observed that mitochondrial interconnectivity in the presence of over-expressed AURKA depends on its capacity to be imported/exported, and on the kinase activity of AURKA itself, as the over-expression of AURKA ΔNter, mitoAURKA or the kinase-dead AURKA Lys162Met have no effect on mitochondrial elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data showing no effect on mitochondrial connectivity with AURKA mutants, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: The role of AURKA in the regulation of mitochondrial morphology is conserved in flies and humans with no differences in mitochondrial connectivity due to the silencing or the overexpression of the kinase.
claims.source: Therefore, the role of AURKA in the regulation of mitochondrial morphology is conserved in flies and humans with no differences in mitochondrial connectivity due to the silencing or the overexpression of the kinase.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both AURKA knockdown and overexpression lead to increased mitochondrial connectivity in both flies and human cells.

claims.claim: When AURKA was downregulated, the abundance of MFN1 and OPA1 increased while the level of DNM1L decreased.
claims.source: When AURKA was downregulated, the abundance of MFN1 and OPA1 increased while the level of DNM1L decreased (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing changes in fusion and fission protein levels upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Downregulation of AURKA lead to an increase of Ser637 phosphorylation of DNM1L, corresponding to an increased cytosolic localisation of DNM1L.
claims.source: We then analysed the phosphorylation state of DNM1L on Ser637, since DNM1L localises in the cytosol when phosphorylated on this residue and to mitochondrial when dephosphorylated (Kashatus et al., 2011; Wai and Langer, 2016). Downregulation of AURKA lead to an increase of Ser637 phosphorylation, corresponding to an increased cytosolic localisation of DNM1L (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing increased DNM1L Ser637 phosphorylation upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial connectivity at interphase could be reverted by normal AURKA expressed at physiological levels, but not by the cytosolic-only AURKA ΔNter.
claims.source: Under these experimental conditions, increased mitochondrial connectivity at interphase could be reverted by normal AURKA expressed at physiological levels. On the contrary, the cytosolic-only AURKA ΔNter did not rescue mitochondrial elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), although this protein retains its catalytic activity and its capacity to phosphorylate RALA on Ser194 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mitochondrial morphology analysis showing rescue by normal AURKA but not AURKA ΔNter, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: When AURKA was over-expressed, an increase of the short isoform of OPA1 (S-OPA1) was observed.
claims.source: When AURKA was over-expressed, we observed the increase of the short isoform of OPA1 (S-OPA1), a phenomenon previously reported to be directly caused by an increased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Mishra et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing increased S-OPA1 upon AURKA overexpression, and supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: A small but significant decrease of the levels of DNM1L and its receptor MFF was observed when AURKA was over-expressed.
claims.source: In addition, we also observed a small but significant decrease of the levels of DNM1L and its receptor MFF (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing decreased DNM1L and MFF levels upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: Nearly 60% of cells with ectopic AURKA showed interconnected mitochondria clustered in the perinuclear region.
claims.source: While analysing mitochondria in tumorigenic cells, we observed that nearly 60% of cells with ectopic AURKA showed interconnected mitochondria clustered in the perinuclear region (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial clustering in cells overexpressing AURKA, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F.

claims.claim: AURKA-positive mitochondrial aggregates are SDS-insoluble as indicated by dot-blot filter retardation assays.
claims.source: As mito-aggresomes, we found these AURKA-positive mitochondrial aggregates to be SDS-insoluble as indicated by dot-blot filter retardation assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on dot-blot filter retardation assay data showing SDS-insoluble AURKA aggregates, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G.

claims.claim: The over-expression of the fly homologue of DNM1L – Drp1 – in flies over-expressing AURKA rescued mitochondrial interconnectivity.
claims.source: In vivo, the over-expression of the fly homologue of DNM1L – Drp1 – in flies over-expressing AURKA rescued mitochondrial interconnectivity analysed with mitoDendra2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data in Drosophila showing rescue of mitochondrial connectivity by Drp1 overexpression, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3H.

claims.claim: A direct interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF was retrieved by localised decrease of the lifetime of AURKA-GFP on mitochondria in FRET/FLIM analyses.
claims.source: Furthermore, we retrieved a direct interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF by localised decrease of the lifetime of AURKA-GFP on mitochondria in FRET/FLIM analyses (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing decreased GFP lifetime indicating proximity between AURKA and DNM1L/MFF, shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF in the AURKA interactome was detected by nanoLC-ESI MS/MS.
claims.source: Accordingly, the interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF in the AURKA interactome was also detected by nanoLC-ESI MS/MS (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data identifying AURKA interactions with DNM1L and MFF, shown in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Over-expressed AURKA directly interacts with the fission proteins DNM1L and MFF and drives mitochondrial elongation.
claims.source: Together, over-expressed AURKA directly interacts with the fission proteins DNM1L and MFF and drives mitochondrial elongation.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes findings from FRET/FLIM and mass spectrometry data showing AURKA interactions with fission proteins.

claims.claim: Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells show low expression levels of AURKA, whereas MDA-MB-468 and T47D express AURKA at higher levels.
claims.source: Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells show low expression levels of AURKA, whereas MDA-MB-468 and T47D express AURKA at higher levels (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data comparing AURKA expression levels across four breast cancer cell lines, shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Mitochondria appeared more fragmented in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, and more elongated in MDA-MB-468 and T47D.
claims.source: When looking at the morphology of the mitochondrial network, mitochondria appeared more fragmented in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, and more elongated in MDA-MB-468 and T47D (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy data showing mitochondrial morphology differences across cell lines, shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: MLN8237 had no effect on mitochondrial length in MDA-MB-468 and T47D cells, which express high levels of AURKA.
claims.source: To correlate this phenotype with the abundance of AURKA, we inhibited the kinase with MLN8237. MLN8237 had no effect on mitochondrial length in MDA-MB-468 and T47D cells, which express high levels of AURKA and where the mitochondrial network is already dramatically interconnected per se.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial morphology after MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: MLN8237 increased mitochondrial length and branching in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, where the abundance of AURKA is low and mitochondria appear fragmented in basal conditions.
claims.source: Conversely, MLN8237 increased mitochondrial length and branching in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, where the abundance of AURKA is low and mitochondria appear fragmented in basal conditions (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial morphology after MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: AURKA plays two opposing functions in mitochondrial dynamics according to its abundance in the cell: contributing to organelle fission when expressed under physiological conditions, and directly increasing mitochondrial fusion when over-expressed.
claims.source: Together, AURKA plays two opposing functions in mitochondrial dynamics according to its abundance in the cell: contributing to organelle fission when expressed under physiological conditions, and directly increasing mitochondrial fusion when over-expressed.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing different effects of AURKA on mitochondrial dynamics depending on expression level.

claims.claim: These roles of AURKA are conserved in four carcinoma cell lines.
claims.source: These roles of AURKA are conserved in four carcinoma cell lines, further increasing the relevance of these results.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on data from four different breast cancer cell lines showing similar AURKA effects on mitochondrial morphology.

claims.claim: The levels of the respiratory complex IV subunits increased in the presence of over-expressed AURKA.
claims.source: Among the levels of steady-state respiratory complexes, western blotting analysis revealed that the levels of the respiratory complex IV subunits increased in the presence of over-expressed AURKA (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing increased complex IV subunit levels upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Increased abundance and activity of the respiratory complex IV are part of a mitochondrial-specific signature of epithelial cancers, which mainly rely on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production.
claims.source: It has been reported that increased abundance and activity of the respiratory complex IV are part of a mitochondrial-specific signature of epithelial cancers, which mainly rely on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production (Whitaker-Menezes et al., 2011; Vyas et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature about epithelial cancer metabolism.

claims.claim: The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was increased when AURKA was over-expressed in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: In this light, we observed that the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) – a measure of mitochondrial respiration – was increased when AURKA was over-expressed in HEK293 cells (Figure 5B) (Whitaker-Menezes et al., 2011; Vyas et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on oxygen consumption measurements showing increased OCR upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The analysis of the interactome of AURKA by proteomics showed that AURKA directly interacts with multiple subunits of all respiratory complexes in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: Although only the steady-state levels of complex IV increased significantly in the presence of ectopic AURKA, the analysis of the interactome of AURKA by proteomics showed that AURKA directly interacts with multiple subunits of all respiratory complexes in HEK293 cells (Supplementary file 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data identifying AURKA interactions with respiratory complex subunits, shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Over-expressed AURKA globally acts on the mitochondrial respiratory chain to increase ATP production.
claims.source: This reinforces the conclusion that over-expressed AURKA globally acts on the mitochondrial respiratory chain to increase ATP production.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of increased complex IV levels, increased OCR, and AURKA interactions with respiratory complex subunits.

claims.claim: The over-expression of AURKA increased the proportion of cells exhibiting ongoing autophagy.
claims.source: The over-expression of AURKA increased the proportion of cells exhibiting ongoing autophagy (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data measuring autophagy markers upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The downregulation of AURKA increased the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
claims.source: On the contrary, the downregulation of AURKA increased the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Figure 5D), which has been proposed to be a complementary system of autophagy for the degradation of selective mitochondrial proteins (Zhu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data measuring proteasome activity upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 5D, and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Increasing levels of red mitoTimer were observed in cells transfected with an AURKA-shRNA, indicating that mitochondrial turnover was attenuated under these conditions.
claims.source: To specifically evaluate the turnover of mitochondria, we calculated the red/green ratio of MitoTimer (Ferree et al., 2013). Increasing levels of red mitoTimer were observed in cells transfected with an AURKA-shRNA (Figure 5E), indicating that mitochondrial turnover was attenuated under these conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on MitoTimer fluorescence measurements showing increased red/green ratio upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 5E, and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ) measured with JC-1 or with TMRM decreased upon AURKA knockdown.
claims.source: Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ) – another indicator of mitochondrial functionality – measured with JC-1 (Figure 5F) or with Tetramethylrhodamine Methyl Ester (TMRM) (Figure 5G) decreased upon AURKA knockdown, further confirming that mitochondria are defective in the absence of AURKA.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data measuring mitochondrial membrane potential with JC-1 and TMRM upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claims.claim: No global effect on the mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate was observed when AURKA was knocked down.
claims.source: Although mitochondria are depolarised after AURKA knockdown, no global effect on the mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate was observed under these conditions (Figure 5H), despite both AURKA knockdown and over-expression have an impact on cell viability as previously published (Figure 5I) (Zhang et al., 2004; Bavetsias and Linardopoulos, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on oxygen consumption measurements showing no change in OCR upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial ATP production did not differ from that of control cells when AURKA was inhibited with MLN8237.
claims.source: In addition, the mitochondrial ATP production did not differ from that of control cells when AURKA was inhibited with MLN8237, corroborating the finding that both silencing and inhibition of AURKA do not alter mitochondrial ATP production (Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on oxygen consumption measurements showing no change in ATP production upon MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: AURKA maintains mitochondrial fission when expressed at physiological levels.
claims.source: In conclusion, our results indicate that AURKA maintains mitochondrial fission when expressed at physiological levels and that mitochondrial interconnectivity in the absence of AURKA is a consequence of a lack of fission.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing increased mitochondrial connectivity upon AURKA knockdown due to lack of fission.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial interconnectivity in the absence of AURKA is a consequence of a lack of fission.
claims.source: In conclusion, our results indicate that AURKA maintains mitochondrial fission when expressed at physiological levels and that mitochondrial interconnectivity in the absence of AURKA is a consequence of a lack of fission.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AURKA knockdown leads to increased mitochondrial connectivity without increased ATP production.

claims.claim: The absence of AURKA results in the mere accumulation of elongated mitochondria without any increase in the energetic capabilities of the mitochondrial network.
claims.source: This results in the mere accumulation of elongated mitochondria without any increase in the energetic capabilities of the mitochondrial network.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AURKA knockdown increases mitochondrial connectivity but does not increase ATP production.

claims.claim: Over-expressed AURKA actively enhances ATP production by promoting mitochondrial interconnectivity.
claims.source: On the contrary, over-expressed AURKA actively enhances ATP production by promoting mitochondrial interconnectivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on data showing increased ATP production and mitochondrial connectivity upon AURKA overexpression.

claims.claim: The molecular mechanisms used by AURKA to regulate mitochondrial dynamics are distinct according to the expression levels of the kinase.
claims.source: In this light, we indeed demonstrate that the molecular mechanisms used by AURKA to regulate mitochondrial dynamics are distinct according to the expression levels of the kinase.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AURKA knockdown and overexpression affect different mitochondrial proteins and pathways.

claims.claim: When AURKA is silenced, fission is inhibited.
claims.source: When AURKA is silenced, fission is inhibited.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing increased DNM1L Ser637 phosphorylation and decreased DNM1L levels upon AURKA knockdown.

claims.claim: In conditions where AURKA is overexpressed, fusion is enhanced and so is the energetic capability of the entire mitochondrial network.
claims.source: In conditions where AURKA is overexpressed, fusion is enhanced and so is the energetic capability of the entire mitochondrial network.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on data showing increased S-OPA1, increased OCR, and increased ATP production upon AURKA overexpression.

claims.claim: The simple interconnectivity of the mitochondrial network is not a direct readout of the energetic capabilities of mitochondria.
claims.source: In conclusion, the modifications induced by AURKA to mitochondrial morphology are multifaceted and, in this context, the simple interconnectivity of the mitochondrial network is not a direct readout of the energetic capabilities of mitochondria.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both AURKA knockdown and overexpression lead to interconnected mitochondria, but only overexpression increases ATP production.

claims.claim: AURKA directly interacts with DNM1L and MFF.
claims.source: The AURKA interactome and FRET by FLIM analyses show that AURKA directly interacts with DNM1L and MFF.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM and mass spectrometry data showing AURKA interactions with DNM1L and MFF.

claims.claim: The physical interaction of AURKA with multiple components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain would require the kinase to be imported into mitochondria to ultimately promote ATP production.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the physical interaction of the kinase with multiple components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, located on the Inner Mitochondrial Membrane, would require the kinase to be imported into mitochondria to ultimately promote ATP production.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that respiratory chain components are on the inner mitochondrial membrane, requiring AURKA to be imported to interact with them.

claims.claim: Increased S-OPA1 is a previously characterised hallmark of augmented mitochondrial respiratory chain activity.
claims.source: Of note, increased S-OPA1 is a previously characterised hallmark of augmented mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Mishra et al., 2014), which further reinforces our conclusion that over-expressed AURKA directly potentiates the functionality of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature about S-OPA1 and respiratory chain activity.

claims.claim: Mitotic AURKA promotes mitochondrial fission through the phosphorylation of RALA on Ser194 in the cytosol.
claims.source: Recent findings showed that mitotic AURKA promotes mitochondrial fission through the phosphorylation of RALA on Ser194 in the cytosol (Kashatus et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature about AURKA's role in mitotic mitochondrial fission.

claims.claim: The kinase is imported into mitochondria regardless of RALA.
claims.source: First, the kinase is imported into mitochondria regardless of RALA.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on data showing AURKA in mitochondria after RALA depletion.

claims.claim: The MTS of AURKA is the only portion of the protein strictly required for the pro-fission role of AURKA in physiological conditions.
claims.source: Second, the MTS of AURKA is the only portion of the protein strictly required for the pro-fission role of AURKA in physiological conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that AURKA ΔNter cannot rescue mitochondrial elongation despite being catalytically active.

claims.claim: A version of AURKA devoid of the MTS is unable to induce organelle fragmentation although it is fully capable of phosphorylating RALA on Ser194.
claims.source: Indeed, a version of AURKA devoid of this fragment is unable to induce organelle fragmentation although it is fully capable of phosphorylating RALA on Ser194.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on data showing AURKA ΔNter cannot rescue mitochondrial morphology but can phosphorylate RALA.

claims.claim: AURKA can impact on mitochondrial functions following two parallel pathways: a RALA-independent pathway during interphase, and by interacting with RALA at mitosis.
claims.source: Therefore, our study demonstrates that AURKA can impact on mitochondrial functions following two parallel pathways: a RALA-independent pathway during interphase, and by interacting with RALA at mitosis (Kashatus et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing RALA-independent mitochondrial import of AURKA and previous knowledge of AURKA-RALA interaction at mitosis.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial pool of AURKA regulates the fusion of interconnected organelles and, by doing so, it controls ATP production.
claims.source: In conclusion, we propose the mitochondrial pool of AURKA regulates the fusion of interconnected organelles and, by doing so, it controls ATP production (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the cumulative data showing AURKA's effects on mitochondrial fusion and ATP production.

claims.claim: Mitochondria with high metabolic capacity might escape turnover through fusion mechanisms and thus sustain the high metabolic needs of cancer cells, potentially representing a selective advantage for epithelial cancer progression.
claims.source: Mitochondria with high metabolic capacity might escape turnover through fusion mechanisms and thus sustain the high metabolic needs of cancer cells, potentially representing a selective advantage for epithelial cancer progression.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism for how AURKA-mediated mitochondrial changes could benefit cancer cells.

claims.claim: Targeting mitochondrial hyperfunctionality together with AURKA inhibition might represent an innovative approach in the development of anti-cancer treatments.
claims.source: Targeting mitochondrial hyperfunctionality together with AURKA inhibition might therefore represent an innovative approach in the development of anti-cancer treatments.

results.result: AURKA co-localizes with mitochondria in MCF7 cells across all cell cycle phases, as demonstrated by co-localization with the mitochondrial marker PMPCB. The specificity of this localization is confirmed by loss of signal upon siRNA-mediated AURKA knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1A) showing co-localization with PMPCB, specificity confirmed by siRNA knockdown, and cell cycle-independent localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). The data provide converging evidence for mitochondrial localization of AURKA.

results.result: AURKA exists as three isoforms (46, 43, and 38 kDa) in HEK293 cells, with the 43 and 38 kDa forms representing mitochondrial cleavage products. PMPCB depletion blocks intra-mitochondrial cleavage, and mass spectrometry identifies cleavage sites at residues 33 and 80-82.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C10 are supported by western blot data showing three AURKA isoforms (Figures 1B, 1C), PMPCB knockdown experiments demonstrating reduced cleavage, and mass spectrometry data identifying specific cleavage sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). The evidence converges to support PMPCB-mediated processing of AURKA in mitochondria.

results.result: AURKA is localized to the mitochondrial matrix as a soluble protein, as demonstrated by transmission electron microscopy, sodium carbonate extraction, and protease protection assays showing degradation patterns similar to the matrix protein PMPCB.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are supported by multiple complementary techniques: TEM showing matrix localization (Figure 1D), biochemical fractionation showing soluble fraction localization (Figure 1E), and protease protection assays (Figure 1F). The convergence of multiple independent methods strongly supports matrix localization.

results.result: AURKA physically interacts with all major TOMM subunits (TOMM20, 22, 40, and 70) as indicated by FRET/FLIM analysis showing decreased donor fluorescence lifetime.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 is supported by FRET/FLIM data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showing decreased GFP lifetime when AURKA is co-expressed with TOMM subunits, indicating physical proximity consistent with protein-protein interactions. The method is appropriate for detecting protein proximity.

results.result: The first 30 amino acids of AURKA are necessary but not sufficient for mitochondrial targeting. N-terminal fragments (1-30 or 1-100 aa) fused to GFP do not localize to mitochondria, while deletion of the first 30 amino acids (AURKA ΔNter) abolishes mitochondrial localization despite retaining catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 are supported by immunofluorescence and western blotting data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-D) showing that N-terminal fragments alone cannot target GFP to mitochondria, while deletion of these residues prevents mitochondrial localization. The retention of catalytic activity in AURKA ΔNter (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) confirms the specific role of the N-terminus in mitochondrial targeting rather than protein folding.

results.result: Mitochondrial import of AURKA is independent of RALA, as RALA depletion does not prevent AURKA entry into mitochondria, though it affects overall AURKA abundance proportionally in both total and mitochondrial fractions.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 are supported by western blotting data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E) showing AURKA in mitochondrial fractions after RALA knockdown. The proportional decrease in both total and mitochondrial AURKA suggests RALA affects AURKA stability rather than mitochondrial import specifically.

results.result: AURKA38 is detected in cytosolic fractions, indicating export from mitochondria after processing. A construct with a canonical MTS (mitoAURKA) is not exported and does not localize to centrosomes, demonstrating that the AURKA MTS has unique export properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by western blotting data showing AURKA38 in cytosolic fractions (Figure 2A) and mitoAURKA exclusively in mitochondrial fractions (Figure 2B). Confocal microscopy confirms differential centrosomal localization (Figure 2C). The comparison between native AURKA and mitoAURKA provides strong evidence for export capability.

results.result: AURKA is enzymatically active in mitochondria, as demonstrated by a FRET biosensor showing autophosphorylation on Thr288. This activation is abolished by the AURKA inhibitor MLN8237.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by FRET/FLIM data (Figures 2D, 2E) showing decreased GFP lifetime indicating autophosphorylation, which is reversed by MLN8237 treatment. The biosensor approach is well-validated and provides direct evidence of kinase activity in mitochondria.

results.result: Kinase activity is required for mitochondrial localization of AURKA, as a kinase-dead mutant (AURKA Lys162Met) is not detected in mitochondrial fractions.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by western blotting data (Figure 2F) showing absence of kinase-dead AURKA in mitochondrial fractions. This suggests that catalytic activity is required for mitochondrial import or retention, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Both AURKA knockdown and overexpression lead to increased mitochondrial connectivity, as demonstrated by TEM, morphological analysis, and mitoDendra2 photoconversion in both human cells and Drosophila. This effect requires AURKA's import/export capability and kinase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: TEM showing elongated mitochondria (Figure 3A), quantitative morphological analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), and mitoDendra2 photoconversion in both human cells and Drosophila (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D). The conservation across species and requirement for specific AURKA properties (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B) strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: AURKA knockdown increases mitochondrial fusion proteins (MFN1, OPA1) and decreases fission proteins (DNM1L), with increased DNM1L Ser637 phosphorylation leading to cytosolic localization. This phenotype can be rescued by normal AURKA but not by cytosolic-only AURKA ΔNter.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by western blotting data showing changes in fusion/fission protein levels (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B) and rescue experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C). The inability of catalytically active AURKA ΔNter to rescue the phenotype demonstrates the importance of mitochondrial localization.

results.result: AURKA overexpression increases S-OPA1 and decreases DNM1L and MFF levels, leading to mitochondrial clustering in ~60% of cells. These clusters are SDS-insoluble aggregates, and overexpression of Drp1 in Drosophila rescues mitochondrial interconnectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by western blotting data (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), quantitative analysis of clustering (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F), dot-blot assays showing insoluble aggregates (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G), and genetic rescue in Drosophila (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H). The convergence of biochemical and genetic evidence supports the conclusion.

results.result: Overexpressed AURKA directly interacts with fission proteins DNM1L and MFF, as demonstrated by FRET/FLIM showing decreased GFP lifetime on mitochondria and mass spectrometry detection in the AURKA interactome.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by two independent methods: FRET/FLIM data (Figure 3E) showing physical proximity and mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 2) identifying these interactions. The convergence of biophysical and biochemical approaches provides strong evidence for direct interactions.

results.result: In four breast cancer cell lines, AURKA expression levels correlate with mitochondrial morphology: low AURKA (Hs578T, MDA-MB-231) correlates with fragmented mitochondria, while high AURKA (MDA-MB-468, T47D) correlates with elongated mitochondria. MLN8237 treatment increases mitochondrial length only in low-AURKA cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 are supported by western blotting data showing differential AURKA expression (Figure 4A) and confocal microscopy with quantitative morphological analysis (Figure 4B) across four cell lines. The differential response to MLN8237 based on baseline AURKA levels provides additional support for the dose-dependent effects of AURKA on mitochondrial dynamics.

results.result: AURKA overexpression increases respiratory complex IV subunit levels and oxygen consumption rate (OCR). Mass spectrometry shows AURKA interacts with multiple subunits of all respiratory complexes, suggesting global effects on the mitochondrial respiratory chain to increase ATP production.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by western blotting data (Figure 5A), oxygen consumption measurements (Figure 5B), and mass spectrometry data (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The convergence of protein abundance, functional measurements, and interaction data supports the conclusion that AURKA enhances respiratory chain function.

results.result: AURKA overexpression increases autophagy, while AURKA knockdown increases ubiquitin-proteasome system activity, attenuates mitochondrial turnover (increased red mitoTimer), and decreases mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by JC-1 and TMRM).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by flow cytometry data measuring autophagy (Figure 5C), proteasome activity (Figure 5D), mitoTimer fluorescence (Figure 5E), and membrane potential (Figures 5F, 5G). The complementary measurements of mitochondrial stress and turnover provide consistent evidence for differential effects of AURKA levels on mitochondrial quality control.

results.result: AURKA knockdown or inhibition does not affect mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate or ATP production despite causing mitochondrial depolarization. This indicates that AURKA maintains mitochondrial fission at physiological levels, and its absence leads to accumulation of elongated mitochondria without increased energetic capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 are supported by oxygen consumption measurements (Figures 5H, 5L) showing no change in OCR despite membrane potential changes. This apparent paradox is explained by the authors' interpretation that AURKA knockdown causes passive accumulation of interconnected mitochondria due to lack of fission, rather than active fusion that would enhance ATP production.

results.result: AURKA regulates mitochondrial dynamics through distinct mechanisms depending on expression level: at physiological levels it promotes fission, while overexpression actively enhances fusion and ATP production. Mitochondrial interconnectivity alone is not a direct indicator of energetic capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 synthesize findings from multiple experiments showing differential effects of AURKA levels on mitochondrial proteins, morphology, and function. The key insight that similar morphological outcomes (interconnected mitochondria) can result from different mechanisms (lack of fission vs. enhanced fusion) with different functional consequences is well-supported by the data.

results.result: AURKA directly interacts with DNM1L and MFF, and its interaction with respiratory chain components on the inner mitochondrial membrane requires mitochondrial import. Increased S-OPA1 is a hallmark of augmented respiratory chain activity, supporting the conclusion that overexpressed AURKA potentiates respiratory chain functionality.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by FRET/FLIM and mass spectrometry data for DNM1L/MFF interactions, and by established knowledge (cited literature) about S-OPA1 as a marker of respiratory chain activity. The logical inference that inner membrane interactions require import is sound.

results.result: AURKA impacts mitochondrial function through two parallel pathways: a RALA-independent pathway during interphase requiring the MTS, and a RALA-dependent pathway at mitosis. The MTS is necessary for the pro-fission role of AURKA at physiological levels, as AURKA ΔNter cannot rescue mitochondrial morphology despite phosphorylating RALA.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 integrate current findings with previous literature (Kashatus et al., 2011) to propose a model of dual AURKA pathways. The data showing RALA-independent import (C21-C22) and the inability of catalytically active AURKA ΔNter to rescue mitochondrial phenotypes (C40) support the existence of distinct mechanisms.

results.result: The authors propose that mitochondrial AURKA regulates fusion of interconnected organelles to control ATP production, potentially allowing mitochondria with high metabolic capacity to escape turnover and sustain cancer cell metabolism. They suggest targeting mitochondrial hyperfunctionality together with AURKA inhibition as a therapeutic approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are speculative proposals based on the cumulative data. While the data support AURKA's role in mitochondrial fusion and ATP production, the specific mechanism of selective mitochondrial escape from turnover and the therapeutic implications are hypothetical and require further validation. The model is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: The study demonstrates that AURKA localizes to and is imported into mitochondria in multiple cancer cell lines, where it impacts mitochondrial dynamics and energy production. At endogenous levels, AURKA induces mitochondrial fragmentation independently of RALA, while overexpression enhances fusion and ATP production, promoting metabolic reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C91 summarize the main findings of the study, which are well-supported by the extensive experimental data across multiple cell lines and model systems. The claims accurately reflect the major conclusions drawn from the results.

results.result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about AURKA's mitotic functions, its role as an oncogene in epithelial cancers, epithelial cancer dependence on mitochondrial ATP, and the mechanisms of mitochondrial fusion and fission. It also notes that AURKA is active at interphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C108 present established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. These background claims provide context for the novel findings and are well-supported by the cited references.
